sections.body_md:
A primal-dual interior-point step solves a smoothed version of the KKT system, then lets the smoothing shrink. For a standard-form linear program the unsmoothed system asks for primal feasibility, dual feasibility, nonnegative \(x\) and \(s\), and complementary products \(x_i s_i = 0\). The smoothed system keeps the two feasibility equations and replaces the products by \(x_i s_i = \mu\) with a positive target, while \(x\) and \(s\) stay positive.

As the target varies, the solutions form the central path. On the path the duality gap \(x^T s\) equals \(n \mu\). Driving the target to zero drives the gap to zero. The quantity under control is the gap, not the distance to a vertex.

The products make the map nonlinear. One iteration linearizes it by Newton at a positive point, for a chosen target, then shortens the step so the updated \(x\) and \(s\) stay positive.

A short-step path follower reduces the duality gap to a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of its initial value in a number of Newton steps on the order of \(\sqrt{n}\) times a logarithm of \(1/\varepsilon\). That count is about the gap. Affine scaling drops the target to zero. A positive target is what pulls the point back toward the central path.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The perturbed system is
\[
A x = b, \qquad A^T y + s = c, \qquad x_i s_i = \mu,
\]
with \(x > 0\), \(s > 0\), and \(\mu > 0\). The gap on the path is \(x^T s = n \mu\). The step is shortened so the next point stays positive.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(x = (4,\ 1)\), \(s = (4,\ 1)\), \(y = 0\), and a cost equal to the slack, so the primal sum is \(5\) and both feasibility residuals are zero. The products are \(16\) and \(1\). Choose the target \(4\), the product of the two primal coordinates. The Newton step that equalizes the products leaves the slacks and the multiplier alone and sends the primal step to \((-3,\ 3)\).

The new primal vector is \((1,\ 4)\). Both products equal \(4\), and the old gap was \(17\).

The gate gap is 8. The new gap is \(1 \cdot 4 + 4 \cdot 1 = 8\), which is \(2 \cdot 4\). Adding the opposite step lands at \((7,\ -2)\), outside the positive orthant. The quantity that moved from \(20\) to \(8\) is the gap.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A sign error in the Newton update is the usual arithmetic slip: the step is added to the current point. Adding its opposite leaves the positive orthant and undoes the linearization. A second slip is to quote \(n \mu\) as a distance to the optimum. It is the duality gap on the central path. A third is to set the target to zero on every step and still call the result a centering iteration. A zero target is the predictor direction. A fourth is to forget to shorten the step. The linear equations can survive a long step while positivity does not. Every coordinate product has to match the target.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Conditional gradient is a different first-order method on a compact convex set. It never forms this perturbed system. It minimizes a linear model and walks toward a vertex, and its guarantee is a function-gap bound of order \(1/k\). The interior-point count above is a bound on the number of Newton steps that shrink a duality gap. The two statements measure different things, on different problems.
